title: How To Handle Return-To-School Misbehavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2021/04/23/how-to-handle-return-to-school-misbehavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses teachers surprised by a wave of misbehavior as students return in person after remote learning, arguing they shouldn't be surprised at all since the dynamic of in-person classrooms is fundamentally different from the online one students grew accustomed to. His core recommendation is to treat the return as if it were literally the first day of school: call a transparent 'do-over,' openly acknowledge that expectations weren't clearly (re)taught, and rebuild every routine from entering the room to transitioning between activities in exacting detail. He frames this reset as neither too harsh nor too late regardless of hybrid schedules, insisting that a bold, cheerful, high-standard restart is the fastest way out of the chaos many teachers were experiencing.
points: Returning students are not the same as their online selves — the 'mute button' and social buffer of remote learning are gone.
Teachers who skipped detailed routine-teaching upon return are advised to explicitly acknowledge the gap rather than push through.
The prescribed fix is a transparent 'do-over': telling students plainly that expectations weren't set clearly and restarting from scratch.
Every basic routine — entering the room, opening laptops, transitioning activities, turning in work — should be retaught in exacting detail.
The reset should be delivered with boldness and good cheer rather than apology, framed as setting a 'sky-high bar of excellence.'
quotes: After all, the students you saw online aren’t the same ones you’re seeing in person. Oh, they have the same names. They look the same.
The upside down has turned right side up. That virtual reality environment you taught in, along with the two-dimensional relationship you had with your students, is gone.
You remember that for all practical purposes the day your students returned to the classroom was the first day of school. And it needed to be treated as such.
You pretend it is the first day of school. You say simply, “I’m not happy with how things are going. It’s my fault, not yours, and here is what we’re going to do about it.
Take control of your classroom with boldness and good cheer. Throw a happy shock to their system by setting a sky-high bar of excellence.
